style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay, a quick summary before the practice.
Everything important about averages, in about three minutes.
Symmetric numbers? Then the average is the middle. No calculation.
And evenly spaced numbers are symmetric too. So it's the middle one, or first plus last, over two. Four, ten, sixteen, twenty-two, twenty-eight... the average is sixteen.
Also, if you add or remove a value equal to the average, nothing changes. And the average always sits between the smallest and the largest value.
Now, the most useful move is to turn it around. Sum equals number times average. Eight values, average seven... the sum is fifty-six.
You don't know the values? Well, you don't need them. Treat every value as the average.
A value joins or leaves? Change the sum, and change what you divide by.
The differences from the average always add up to zero. Above the average equals below it.

Seventy-seven, eighty-five, eighty-six, and one missing, with an average of eighty. That's minus three, plus five, plus six... plus eight too many above. So the missing one is eight below. Seventy-two.
Numbers near a round number? Work only with the differences. Around sixty, the differences add up to four, over four values is one... so the average is sixty-one.
One value changes? Share the change over all the values. Plus twelve over four values is plus three.
Every value changes the same way? Then the average changes the same way.
And both at once? Same order. Times two, then plus five. And with ages, an average of twenty-four now is twenty-seven in three years.

Okay, the largest value. Make the others as small as possible. Six positive integers, average eight, so the sum is forty-eight. Five ones? Only if they're allowed to be equal... then it's forty-three. Different integers? One, two, three, four, five, so it's thirty-three.
And how many were there before? Compare the new value to the new average. Then share that extra among the old values.
And check, is it before the new value joined, or after?
On the exam it just says "average". So you have to notice the weights yourself.
Each value times its weight. Then divide by the sum of the weights... not by the number of values.
Now, the see-saw. The distances are the weights, flipped. Weights four to one, distances one to four.
Fifty and a hundred. That's a gap of fifty, so five parts of ten. One part from the heavy side... sixty.
Only two kinds of items? Start everyone at the low value. Then share the extra.
Combining groups? The size of each group is its weight. Reduce the ratio first.
And before you calculate... the average of forty and sixty is fifty only if the groups are equal. Otherwise, the answer is on the side of the bigger group.
So, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: taking the average of two group averages when the groups aren't equal, dividing by the wrong number, and counting before instead of after.
Good luck.
